        Station

        Star map

        How this works

        The loop

        Earn ISK → fit a better ship → reach more dangerous space → earn faster. Mine asteroids, haul goods between stations, run missions, build things, or take what others built. When a ship dies, it and everything on it are gone forever. Keep spare ships and ISK at stations.

        Flying

        Mouse steers · W/S throttle · Shift boost · Tab targets. The OVERVIEW (right panel) is your world: click a row, then Warp / Approach / Orbit. E docks or interacts · N star map · J jumps a gate · 1–8 cycle fitted modules. Green systems (0.5+) are policed; red ones pay better and shoot back.

        At a station

        Market trades · Fitting arms your ship within powergrid/CPU · Missions pay ISK and standing · Skills train in real time even offline · Industry turns minerals and hours into hardware · Insurance softens the next loss.

        Ships are their parts

        Every ship is built from parts on a grid, and hits land on the part they strike. Lose a thruster and the ship yaws toward the dead engine under power; lose the frame that holds a wing and the wing drifts away. Heat is the real limit: reactors, drives and guns make it, and only radiators shed it. G deploys them (fast cooling, fragile) or retracts them (safe, on a heat clock). Past 100% parts start failing; past 130% the crew cooks. Build and refit ships in the station Shipyard; wrecks drop salvaged parts.

        Titans

        Kilometre-long capital ships with spinning habitat rings and a hangar you can fly into — line up with the lit bay and land on a green pad. Strip a titan's radiators and it cooks itself. Your own titan: land in its hangar, E takes the bridge, T toggles tactical view, L launches your fighter.

        Relativity

        Light is slow here (3 km/s) and gravity is real. Near a black hole or a moon, flight turns ballistic: gravity pulls, W burns along the nose, S retro, Space matches the local frame, and the green arc is the nav computer's prediction (gold when a flyby will gain speed). Deep in a black hole's well your clock runs slow — the top panel reads it as "1 hour here = N hours outside" and the whole galaxy (skills, jobs, orders, markets, structures, factions) runs at the outside rate. H holds an orbit (nose prograde, so tides compress the hull); below 3 Rs no orbit holds by itself, and every second costs propellant and heat. Long, thin hulls break in the tides. The horizon is final. Wormholes show the far side; each transit spends stability by mass — the panel says whether your fleet fits. On a titan's bridge, U opens mass-driver fire control: a relativistic slug shatters moons and scars planets for good. One star is going supernova on the date on the title screen. F8 sets lensing quality.

        Planets

        Inhabited worlds show it: city lights on the night side, orbital habitats and shuttle traffic, and in high sec a space elevator. Each planet's capital stands near its first landing site; smaller settlements dot some of the others (the survey card says which). Cities have a spaceport pad beside the landing zone — land on it and press E to sell ore and relics, refuel, patch the hull or buy local goods. Rooftops are solid. A city under an RKV strike stays a ruin.

        Warp to a planet, hold orbit, press E — one site is always ready — and descend. Land gently on flat ground. You start with a rover in the hold: R deploys it. Drive it (P prospects) to drill deposits, grab salvage crates, ride geyser vents for gas, clear fauna nests, and run the timed circuit through the amber rings for ISK. Settlements on green worlds buy ore and artifacts on the spot. B anchors a mining outpost. Climb past 900 m to leave.

        Multiplayer

        Everyone playing shares space. Pilots in your system appear with nametags — in low/null sec (below 0.5) they can shoot you, and you them. The lobby on the title screen hosts co-op and versus matches.

        The hint bar above the radar always suggests your next move — the × on it (or this panel) turns it off and on.
